new_statements.quote: Disyllabic morphemes are assigned stress on the first syllable. Morphemes of more than two syllables are assigned stress on the first syllable and then on following alternating syllables except the final rightmost syllable which is not stressed. [...] When morphemes of two or more syllables are attached, to construct a word, stress is still placed on the first syllable of each morpheme. Alternating syllables that intervene between these stressed syllables are also stressed except when this would result in adjacent stressed syllables. The final syllable in a word is not stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (Kurrama kurr1243 is not in the catalog and has no stress statement held by the project; the bibliography row for Austin 1988 is tagged 'read: notes on stress' but no statement was filed). Hill's rule is the standard Ngayarda/Central Pilbara initial-stress pattern with morpheme-initial and alternating further stresses, final syllable unstressed; consistent with Wordick 1982 on the Yindjibarndi co-dialect (that entry was read as silent for Kurrama specifically).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and morphology-sensitive: every morpheme of two or more syllables is stressed on its first syllable; within a morpheme of three or more syllables stress then alternates rightward (1st, 3rd, 5th..) but the final syllable of the morpheme/word is never stressed; in a suffixed word each polysyllabic morpheme keeps initial stress and intervening syllables are stressed on an alternating count unless that would create a clash; monosyllabic suffixes are stressed only when they fall on an alternating beat between morpheme-initial stresses. Hence a monomorphemic word has initial stress (kurri, majarra, kakarlurlu with 1st+3rd). Hill marks all stresses alike (underlining) and does not rank primary vs secondary; he calls the account preliminary ('not a detailed study of stress patterning').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not distinguished from primary by the author: all stressed syllables (word-initial, morpheme-initial, alternating) are marked identically by underlining; rhythmically the non-initial stresses (3rd, 5th syllable; first syllable of each following polysyllabic morpheme; monosyllabic suffixes on an alternating beat) function as the secondary stresses of the usual Pama-Nyungan pattern, with clash avoidance and an unstressed word-final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: (p.25) the monosyllabic causative -ma-L 'will often attract stress' instead of the first syllable of a following disyllabic inflection (mirnu-ma-nmarta, murlimurli-ma-langu), but not if that would leave three unstressed syllables after it (murlimurli-ma-nnguli-ngu, mirnu-ma-rnumarnu); long vowels /aa/ arising across a morpheme boundary 'break', with stress on the second (suffix-initial) vowel (pawa-arta, ngarrka-ayi); some morpheme-internal long vowels in the second syllable of trisyllables also break (ngunhaatu, wantaawa), giving an effective four-syllable word stressed on 1st and 3rd -- 'not a firm analysis.. requires more study' (pp.25-26).
new_statements.identity_note: Kurrama (Gurama), Central Pilbara group, treated by O'Grady 1966 and Wordick 1982 as a co-dialect of Yindjibarndi; Hill's data are Alan Dench's 1980s-90s recordings of Algy Paterson and Judy July plus Hill's 2007 fieldwork with Maudie Dowton and Thomas Cox; Hill states Kurrama phonology 'varies only a little' from Wordick's Yindjibarndi and gives his own brief stress section for Kurrama specifically.

sources.note: Language page: Dench worked with the Kurrama Elders Group from 1990; his texts were used in 2006 to produce the Kurrama Dictionary and Sketch Grammar; fewer than 10 speakers in 2002. Brochure: generic sounds/syllables primer for Pilbara languages; nothing on stress (scanned of page 2 checked).

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas. 1993. Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal languages south of the Kimberley Region. Pacific Linguistics C-124. Entry 4.4.5 Kurrama, pp. 115-116; annotated bibliography pp. 310-311, 329.
sources.note: Bibliographic handbook, no phonology. States 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None, but see Wordick's (1982) grammar of Yindjibarndi, which is very closely related to Kurrama'; 'Practical spelling system: None, but the Yindjibarndi system may be used'; cites Dench (1990 p.c.) that Kurrama and Yindjibarndi are 'phonologically, morphologically and syntactically very similar' and names five dialects (Yarnarri, Yinyjiwarnti Kurrama, Mijarranypa, Marntartka, Ngamangamara). Lists Hale 1959 'Gurama fieldnotes' MS, Dench 1990 MS wordlist/texts, Dench 1987a Appendix A comparative phonology. Nothing on stre…

sources.citation: Dench, Alan. 1987. Martuthunira: a language of the Pilbara region of Western Australia. PhD thesis, Australian National University. Appendix A 'The phonological history of the Ngayarda languages', A.3 'Phonological changes in Kurrama', pp. 522-523; sec. 2.6 Stress pp. 97-105 (Martuthunira).
sources.note: The only Kurrama-specific phonology is diachronic (stop lenition parallels Yindjibarndi; syllable-final laterals fortify to stops: *pulka > putka, *wirlkara > wirtkaa, *-lkaji > -tkayi). The stress section (2.6) is about Martuthunira (initial stress, disyllabic pattern, lexical stress marks). No statement about Kurrama stress.

sources.citation: Wordick, F. J. F. 1982. The Yindjibarndi language. Pacific Linguistics C-71. Canberra: ANU. sec. 1.1.4 (p. 6) and sec. 2.3.2 'Accent' (pp. 41-42).
sources.note: Describes YINDJIBARNDI accent only: within the word, stress and pitch combine into three degrees; in words with short vowels the pattern is 1 3 2 3 2 3 (primary on syllable 1, secondary on odd syllables), long vowels in even syllables attract the accent. On Kurrama it says (p. 6) 'The two languages possess identical phonological systems' but 'I have not included a description of Kurrama in this book.' No Kurrama stress statement — the earlier scan's hope that this grammar covers Kurrama is not borne out.
